discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy beyond the Galaxy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led the construction of IceCube, a cubic-kilometre neutrino telescope in the Antarctic ice, through decades of patient development from AMANDA onward. In 2013 IceCube reported the first evidence of a diffuse flux of high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, well above the atmospheric background, later confirmed at high significance. This was followed by the coincident detection of a neutrino with the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017), evidence of neutrino emission from the active galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and the observation of neutrinos from the Galactic plane (2023). Together these results opened a new window on the universe: neutrinos now trace the most energetic cosmic accelerators and the origin of cosmic rays. As in the Kamiokande detection of supernova neutrinos, a large and long-term detector built for basic science has created a new field of astronomy. Halzen's scientific vision and leadership were decisive.
